WOMEN WHO KILL

By: Nicky Troll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Cop that called hits on loved ones for big insurance payouts, is one of many women who kill for cash – we explore this new criminal trend

Unique Selling Point:
** INTERESTING ANGLE TO UNPACK A GRIPPING NEWS STORY


Summary:
While the country is gripped by the antics unfolding in a Gauteng Court around the case of former police constable Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu, an alleged serial killer accused of murdering her family members in return for insurance payouts, we dig deeper into the driving forces behind women who kill.

Ndlovu may not have pulled the trigger, but she orchestrated the murder of at least 6 people.

A shocking trend reveals how the masterminds calling hits for financial benefit are almost always women – changing the face of the serial killer profile in South Africa.


Further information:
Undercover footage allegedly captured by an undercover police officer who had hidden the recording device in the car in which he, Ndlovu and another recruited “hitman” were travelling – exposed Ndlovu for the killer she is.
The trio was headed to Bushbuckridge, where Ndlovu was due to show them her sister’s house. She allegedly wanted the two men to burn her sister, Joyce, and her five children alive in the house.
In her own words, Ndlovu said they should “leave no witnesses behind”.
In the recording, Ndlovu explained how she had earlier checked herself into hospital to create an alibi and then secured a day pass to leave the premises.
En route to Bushbuckridge, they stopped at a garage in Middelburg, Mpumalanga, where she purchased two litres of petrol and handed it to the undercover officer. The petrol was meant to be used to ignite the flames that would wipe out six of her family members.
It was also in this footage, taken during their five-hour drive from Johannesburg to Bushbuckridge, that she allegedly provided a motive for wanting her sister dead.
“You know I don’t have money,” Ndlovu is heard saying, addressing the alleged hitman, Njabulo Kunene. “You know I’m doing this so I can get a bit of money. You’ve seen that my car is on the brink of being repossessed. I don’t have money,” she said.
Ndlovu seemed unshaken and nonchalant about knowing her sister’s children would also die in the fire.
When asked by the undercover officers whether the policies she had also covered the children, she replied: “It won’t pay out for the children, only for [the mother]. But they cannot be left behind since they will be there too. You know that sparing them will mean leaving behind witnesses. So when a house burns down, everyone burns with it.”
She had allegedly hoped the fire would be ruled as an accident and she would cash in on a large sum of money from the insurance policies.
Ndlovu was nabbed moments after she had pointed out her sister’s house to the “hitmen” and boarded a taxi back to Johannesburg, where she was rushing to return to the Carstenhof Hospital in Midrand to cement her alibi.
A screengrab from the video showing Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu, a former policewoman, passing a two-litre bottle of petrol to an undercover police officer.
Image: Screengrab from video
Backtrack
It was through her work as a police officer at the Thembisa South police station that Ndlovu allegedly met two “hitmen” she hired to kill her mother, sisters, nieces and nephews.
The men, Kunene and Lakhiwe Mkhize, were crucial to the state’s case as Ndlovu’s trial played out in the court.
The court heard Kunene had been arrested several years ago by Ndlovu on a gun possession charge. He was later cleared of the charge. He alleged that in 2017 he was approached by Ndlovu, who said she wanted him to kill his sister, Gladys.
Gladys lived in Pholosong in Thembisa. Shocked by this request, Kunene told his friend Mkhize about this. Mkhize was present when Ndlovu allegedly met Kunene to follow up on her request and he was roped into the murder plot. Together, they drove to Gladys’s house.
They claimed they were promised R15,000 for Gladys’s life. They were given R800 as a down payment for petrol. However, they never carried out the plot and avoided Ndlovu.
In February 2018, Ndlovu approached Mkhize and allegedly said this time she had another target, her elderly mother, Maria Mushwana, who lived in Thulamahashe, Buckbuckridge. Mkhize was allegedly paid R2,600 for the job and taken to Bushbuckridge, where he was shown the house.
Mkhize, however, failed to execute the killing.
He said when he arrived at the elderly woman’s house, he was moved by how vulnerable and fragile she was. Instead, he asked for a glass of water and left, taking off with Ndlovu’s money.
The 80-year-old Mushwana is expected to be among those who will testify in Ndlovu’s defence.
A month after the alleged botched hit on her mother, Ndlovu is alleged to have returned to her initial “hitman”, Kunene, and told him she wanted her sister Joyce and her five children — the youngest was five months old — killed. She allegedly wanted them burnt alive in their Bushbuckridge home.
Ndlovu had insinuated that none of the six should survive.
Kunene agreed, but was disturbed by Ndlovu’s heinous plot, so he approached the police and shared the information.
Police set up a sting operation and sent Kunene back to Ndlovu with an undercover police officer, who posed as Kunene’s accomplice.
Alleged trail of bodies
The state alleged that Ndlovu had, over the years, cashed more than R1.4m after the deaths of six of her loved ones. Her victims were listed as:
• Her cousin Witness Madala Homu. He was murdered in March 2012 on his way home from work. His body was found dumped in Johannesburg and he had sustained head injuries. The state alleged Ndlovu had hired a hitman to carry out this crime. She claimed more than R131,000 from policies after his death, but did not assist his family with the funeral.
• Her sister Audrey Somisa Ndlovu. She was found poisoned and strangled to death in her rented room in Thembisa in June 2013. Ndlovu is alleged to have taken out numerous policies in her sister’s name. She is also alleged to have called the insurance companies while posing as Audrey. It was then that she listed herself as a beneficiary to Audrey’s policies. Ndlovu claimed more than R717,000 in insurance.
• Her boyfriend Yingwani Maurice Mabasa. He died in October 2015 after being stabbed more than 80 times. His body was dumped near the Olifantsfontein police station. None of his valuables were taken. The state alleged Ndlovu had taken out several policies in Mabasa’s name and had recruited a man to take out life-insurance policies while posing as Mabasa. On some insurance policies she had listed Mabasa as her spouse and herself as the beneficiary. She paid the premiums and cashed more than R416,000 after Mabasa’s death. She contributed R40,000 to his funeral.
• Her niece Zanele Motha. She died in June 2016 after claims she had been attacked in the streets of Kempton Park. At the time Motha was visiting Ndlovu. Two days before her death, she had been treated at the Thembisa Hospital for scratches and bruises which she said came after she was hit by a bicycle. On her second admission, Motha was rushed to the Arwyp Medical Centre in Kempton Park, where she was found to have suffered fractured ribs and a damaged liver. Ndlovu allegedly cashed in almost R120,000 in policies for Motha. She did not assist the family when it came to burial costs.
• Her nephew Mayeni Mashaba. He died in April 2017, on the same day he had arranged to meet Ndlovu in Daveyton, Ekurhuleni. His body was found dumped near Olifantsfontein with major head injuries. His cellphone records put him in the same location as Ndlovu at the time of his death. It was not immediately clear whether she had claimed on policies after his death.
• Her nephew Brilliant Mashego. He was the son of Audrey, whom Ndlovu is accused of killing several years earlier. Mashego died in January 2018 after allegedly catching wind of news that Ndlovu had pocketed cash after his mother’s death. Ndlovu had taken Mashego under her wing with a promise that she would help him find a job. Mashego’s body was dumped at a marketplace in Bushbuckridge a few days after he had left home to allegedly meet Ndlovu. It was unclear whether she claimed on any policies after Mashego’s death.

The state provided Nomia Ndlovu's family tree as evidence. All relatives with a red cross have died, allegedly through her actions. Those with smaller stars next to their names were alleged to have been on her hit list. Those with purple crosses also died but their deaths have not necessarily been linked to Ndlovu.
Image: Supplied
Last week, the state closed its case. Besides leading evidence from the alleged hitmen, the prosecution led testimony from analysts at insurance companies Ndlovu is alleged to have defrauded, cellphone tech experts who placed Ndlovu around some of the crime scenes and her family members, some of whom survived the alleged killing spree.
Now Ndlovu is expected to start presenting her defence. Her brother, Director, is expected to testify for her.
The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder, attempted murder or conspiring to commit murder, defeating the ends of justice and fraud.
During her bail application, she indicated she accepted only the charges relating to the conspiracy to commit the murder of Joyce and her five children. She said, however, she would explain this during her trial.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: This is a story of carefully orchestrated killings - riddled with deception and fuelled by greed.

LINK: Hitmen, life insurance fraud and big cash payouts, these are the elements driving a new criminal trend of women killing for financial benefits. Women are the masterminds - pulling these intricate strings.

GARTH: If you take a look at the profile of the individuals involved, it's pure evil.

VO: At the centre of this story, is 46 year old Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu – this former cop stands accused of murder, conspiracy to commit murder, fraud and the obstruction of justice.

Ndlovu faces 20 charges, linked to alleged funeral and life insurance payouts of about R1.4 million and a trail of at least 6 dead bodies. But these aren’t any dead bodies - the alleged victims were her sister, her boyfriend and other family members she took out life insurance for.

Journalist Naledi Shange has extensively covered the trial.

NALEDI: Nomia Ndlovu is the exact opposite of what you would imagine a serial killer to be a woman, a police officer, a person who was a mother herself.

VO: Even though Ndlovu may not have physically been responsible for the alleged murders, if convicted, she still gets serial killer status. Giada del Fabbro is a clinical psychologist.

GIADA: When we look at serial murderers modus operandi,// someone might use shooting or stabbing or strangling, in this case, if she's convicted of the murders, then her method would be using a hitman.

VO: It’s a common trend in female serial killer cases, as definitions have broadened the scope.

GIADA: When you're dealing with a psychopathic person, more often than not, the use of a hitman is the method. And it's really about trying to increase the chances of not getting caught.

VO: The alleged killing spree started in 2012 - first was Ndlovu’s cousin Witness Madala Homu who died of head injuries - she claimed roughly R131 000 in death benefits. Then she turned to her sister Audrey Somisa Ndlovu who was poisoned and strangled to death in 2013 - there she cashed in on policies totalling around R717 000.

Two years later, Ndlovu is accused of setting her sights on her lover - at least 16 policies were opened in Maurice Mabasa’s name.

LINK: Mabasa survived previous attempts on his life, including a fire in the bedroom where he was sleeping. But in October 2015, his luck ran out.

VO: He was stabbed around 80 times. Mabasa’s body was discovered on a road in Oliefantsfontein, close to his brother Justice Mabasa’s home.

JUSTICE: If you look at it, you can see that, yeah, there's a foul play. // You could see that this person was with these people who killed them for a long time. Not just someone just came by it with you. Stabbed you and run, no.

VO: At the time, Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu was not linked to the murder.

JUSTICE: I did not suspect her. Based on the fact that she was a cop, she cannot put their life into a situation of of dirtying hands or anything.

VO: While Mabasa would be proven wrong in years to come, he recalls though, there were some red flags.

JUSTICE: I received several calls from different insurance companies who wanted me to confirm that she was the wife. //that's when all these things // turn into disaster // there was rumors flying around that, you know, there's something wrong here. This person has got so many policies.

VO: Some policies did not pay out, because the couple were never married. In the end, Ndlovu allegedly got about R416 000 from policies she took out on her lover’s life and Mabasa’s work benefits.

Death Benefit Fraud has become a nefarious source of income for criminal networks. Garth de Klerk is from the Insurance Crime Bureau. He explains, it’s not uncommon for these life insurance killers to strike more than once.

GARTH: What we see as a trend is the first one appears to be easy. It appears that they've gotten away with it. The second one then becomes sort of practice for the third and the fourth and the fifth.

VO: Ndlovu’s next alleged victim was her niece, Zanele Motha, in 2016.

LINK: Her life was worth just one hundred and twenty thousand rand tunes over, while the circumstances around her death are still not clear. Her death has left her partner and her children devastated.

VO: Jabu Nhlapo was Zanele Motha’s partner, they had three children together.

JABU: I don't think no one could take care of them as she did // So it was painful, still painful to them. It will always be painful in for us. And we have in the family, it's difficult. No, I'm I'm alone. I'm a mother and I'm a father. It's difficult.

VO: Looking back, Nhlapo remembers feeling uncomfortable when Motha’s aunt, Ndlovu, wanted to get her life cover.

JABU: I didn't like it. I don't know. Maybe the gut feeling

VO: According to the police investigation, three separate policies were taken out in January, March and May 2016. Zanele Motha mysteriously died in June 2016 while visiting her aunt, Ndlovu.

JABU: For me it was all staged. I believe it then before she was arrested, and even now.

VO: Two more family members would be added to Ndlovu’s alleged list of victims - first her nephew Manyeni Mashaba in April 2017, and then another nephew Brilliant Mashego in January 2018.

While both had life insurance policies on their names, no claims were paid out.

Killing for cash has become a lucrative income stream. In 2020 the insurance industry recorded 264.3 million rand in 388 fraudulent death benefit claims . While many of these claims are stopped before pay out, some may go undetected initially.

GARTH: When you commit to financial fraud, the financial motivation will never be enough. You will always be tempted to do more and you'll always get caught.// It's just a matter of time.

LINK: In 2018, the tables were turned and alleged hitmen tipped off the police about Ndlovu’s next plot targeting her sister and her sister's children. The police then launched a covert operation.

VO: An undercover cop travelled with Ndlovu and the so-called hitman she had recruited, to Bushbuckridge. Ndlovu was allegedly going to point out her sister Joyce’s house, for the hit.

They stopped at a filling station in Middleburg to buy petrol for the job. In the video, Ndlovu wanted the house set alight.

Undercover cop: “So will the policies also pay out for her children or?”
Rosemary: “It won’t pay out for the children, only for her. But they cannot be left behind since they will be there too. And you know that sparing them will mean leaving behind witnesses. So when a house burns down, everyone burns with it. “

GIADA: that cold, callous. Matter of fact way in which she's describing it // using people as a means to an end instrumentally. And I think in in in her mind, it was it was very justified what she was doing and that the need to gain financially took precedence over over everything else.

VO: During the covert sting, Ndlovu confirmed her motivation was financial.

ROSEMARY: You know I don’t have money. You know I’m doing this so I can get a bit of money.

VO: Ndlovu was arrested the day this recording was made. She claims she didn’t want the so-called hitmen to actually go through with the hit.

Despite this, she is facing attempted murder charges for allegedly arranging hits on her sister Joyce, along with her children and, more shockingly also calling a hit on her very own mother. Shange met the family in Bushbuckrigde this past week.

NALEDI: It's a family that's literally been torn apart by all of these murders and attempted murders. One of the questions that I asked was how she feels towards her sister. And she answered. I never thought that one day she would want to prey on me.

VO: In an interesting twist, Ndlovu’s mother testified in her defence - despite allegedly being one of her daughter’s targets.

GIADA: no one wants to believe that their child is capable of doing something like this // even to conceptualise the fact that one of your children would be responsible for the murder of your other children and your grand children - I think that’s very hard for someone // there’ a large amount of denial//

VO: While the state has wrapped up its case, Ndlovu has maintained her innocence, pleading not guilty on all charges.

NALEDI: Around 51 state witnesses have testified, and according to Nomia, all 51 of them have lied at one point or the other. //Everyone has lied. That is her story.

VO: The prosecution presented what seems to be a comprehensive case with a range of witnesses connecting the dots in Ndlovu’s alleged web of deception .

De Klerk adds the insurance industry’s forensic teams determined the quantum of claims.

GARTH: The South African police services// gathered evidence on her and then they approached us to say, Please, can we tie together //from the insurance point of view //how many insurance claims had she put together. there's a whole tree around it as to where the money went how it flowed and who were the ultimate beneficiaries.

VO: WIth public interest growing in the case, it appeared that Ndlovu was playing into the spotlight.

NALEDI: She's completely flipped scripts.

VO: Her timing was impeccable if not suspicious, notes Shange.

NALEDI: We’ve noticed is that her falling ill and her being unable to stand the heat in the courtroom is sometimes usually comes at a very crucial time during the state's questioning

VO: Del Fabbro observed that Ndlovu’s antics could be a manipulative attempt to tip the scales in her favour.

GIADA: It may be that she could be trying to be perceived as perhaps unstable. // although it’ll be very difficult to argue for given the meticulous and calculated ways that those crimes were planned out.

VO: The alleged crimes have left the families of the victims gripped by fear.

NALEDI: The thing about Nomia’s Network, we have no idea how far it stretches.


JUSTICE: What if she doesn't get the full conviction? We as the family, we are not safe

VO: Del Fabbro observes serial killers who kill for money, often view people as a means to an end.

GIADA: We are talking about personality structure which is not very capable of empathy //and who really is about surviving and meeting her own needs at any cost. And in this case, the cost was her family.
CLAIRE REMORSE?
GIADA: Wouldn't hold my breath. // you may see self-pity, but you won't see remorse. It will look the same, potentially. Although I think if you spent enough time, you'd see that it's quite superficial.

VO: Ndlovu’s showmanship is not winning over any fans.

JUSTICE: The way in which is just she's taking everyone or the courts for for a ride, It's it's so it's so painful I never suspected that she would be this. This this mean, this, evil.

VO: Even with Ndlovu on trial, Nhlapo doubts whether a conviction will ever bring him peace.

JABU: I don't think that's enough because I'm I'm being taxed money to pay her food at prison that hurts me.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 04 October 2021 Script: STRUCTURE VO: This is a story of carefully orchestrated killings - riddled with deception and fuelled by greed. LINK: Hitmen, life insurance fraud and big cash payouts, these are the elements driving a new criminal trend of women killing for financial benefits. Women are the masterminds - pulling these intricate strings. GARTH: If you take a look at the profile of the individuals involved, it's pure evil. VO: At the centre of this story, is 46 year old Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu – this former cop stands accused of murder, conspiracy to commit murder, fraud and the obstruction of justice. Ndlovu faces 20 charges, linked to alleged funeral and life insurance payouts of about R1.4 million and a trail of at least 6 dead bodies. But these aren’t any dead bodies - the alleged victims were her sister, her boyfriend and other family members she took out life insurance for. Journalist Naledi Shange has extensively covered the trial. NALEDI: Nomia Ndlovu is the exact opposite of what you would imagine a serial killer to be a woman, a police officer, a person who was a mother herself. VO: Even though Ndlovu may not have physically been responsible for the alleged murders, if convicted, she still gets serial killer status. Giada del Fabbro is a clinical psychologist. GIADA: When we look at serial murderers modus operandi,// someone might use shooting or stabbing or strangling, in this case, if she's convicted of the murders, then her method would be using a hitman. VO: It’s a common trend in female serial killer cases, as definitions have broadened the scope. GIADA: When you're dealing with a psychopathic person, more often than not, the use of a hitman is the method. And it's really about trying to increase the chances of not getting caught. VO: The alleged killing spree started in 2012 - first was Ndlovu’s cousin Witness Madala Homu who died of head injuries - she claimed roughly R131 000 in death benefits. Then she turned to her sister Audrey Somisa Ndlovu who was poisoned and strangled to death in 2013 - there she cashed in on policies totalling around R717 000. Two years later, Ndlovu is accused of setting her sights on her lover - at least 16 policies were opened in Maurice Mabasa’s name. LINK: Mabasa survived previous attempts on his life, including a fire in the bedroom where he was sleeping. But in October 2015, his luck ran out. VO: He was stabbed around 80 times. Mabasa’s body was discovered on a road in Oliefantsfontein, close to his brother Justice Mabasa’s home. JUSTICE: If you look at it, you can see that, yeah, there's a foul play. // You could see that this person was with these people who killed them for a long time. Not just someone just came by it with you. Stabbed you and run, no. VO: At the time, Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu was not linked to the murder. JUSTICE: I did not suspect her. Based on the fact that she was a cop, she cannot put their life into a situation of of dirtying hands or anything. VO: While Mabasa would be proven wrong in years to come, he recalls though, there were some red flags. JUSTICE: I received several calls from different insurance companies who wanted me to confirm that she was the wife. //that's when all these things // turn into disaster // there was rumors flying around that, you know, there's something wrong here. This person has got so many policies. VO: Some policies did not pay out, because the couple were never married. In the end, Ndlovu allegedly got about R416 000 from policies she took out on her lover’s life and Mabasa’s work benefits. Death Benefit Fraud has become a nefarious source of income for criminal networks. Garth de Klerk is from the Insurance Crime Bureau. He explains, it’s not uncommon for these life insurance killers to strike more than once. GARTH: What we see as a trend is the first one appears to be easy. It appears that they've gotten away with it. The second one then becomes sort of practice for the third and the fourth and the fifth. VO: Ndlovu’s next alleged victim was her niece, Zanele Motha, in 2016. LINK: Her life was worth just one hundred and twenty thousand rand tunes over, while the circumstances around her death are still not clear. Her death has left her partner and her children devastated. VO: Jabu Nhlapo was Zanele Motha’s partner, they had three children together. JABU: I don't think no one could take care of them as she did // So it was painful, still painful to them. It will always be painful in for us. And we have in the family, it's difficult. No, I'm I'm alone. I'm a mother and I'm a father. It's difficult. VO: Looking back, Nhlapo remembers feeling uncomfortable when Motha’s aunt, Ndlovu, wanted to get her life cover. JABU: I didn't like it. I don't know. Maybe the gut feeling VO: According to the police investigation, three separate policies were taken out in January, March and May 2016. Zanele Motha mysteriously died in June 2016 while visiting her aunt, Ndlovu. JABU: For me it was all staged. I believe it then before she was arrested, and even now. VO: Two more family members would be added to Ndlovu’s alleged list of victims - first her nephew Manyeni Mashaba in April 2017, and then another nephew Brilliant Mashego in January 2018. While both had life insurance policies on their names, no claims were paid out. Killing for cash has become a lucrative income stream. In 2020 the insurance industry recorded 264.3 million rand in 388 fraudulent death benefit claims . While many of these claims are stopped before pay out, some may go undetected initially. GARTH: When you commit to financial fraud, the financial motivation will never be enough. You will always be tempted to do more and you'll always get caught.// It's just a matter of time. LINK: In 2018, the tables were turned and alleged hitmen tipped off the police about Ndlovu’s next plot targeting her sister and her sister's children. The police then launched a covert operation. VO: An undercover cop travelled with Ndlovu and the so-called hitman she had recruited, to Bushbuckridge. Ndlovu was allegedly going to point out her sister Joyce’s house, for the hit. They stopped at a filling station in Middleburg to buy petrol for the job. In the video, Ndlovu wanted the house set alight. Undercover cop: “So will the policies also pay out for her children or?” Rosemary: “It won’t pay out for the children, only for her. But they cannot be left behind since they will be there too. And you know that sparing them will mean leaving behind witnesses. So when a house burns down, everyone burns with it. “ GIADA: that cold, callous. Matter of fact way in which she's describing it // using people as a means to an end instrumentally. And I think in in in her mind, it was it was very justified what she was doing and that the need to gain financially took precedence over over everything else. VO: During the covert sting, Ndlovu confirmed her motivation was financial. ROSEMARY: You know I don’t have money. You know I’m doing this so I can get a bit of money. VO: Ndlovu was arrested the day this recording was made. She claims she didn’t want the so-called hitmen to actually go through with the hit. Despite this, she is facing attempted murder charges for allegedly arranging hits on her sister Joyce, along with her children and, more shockingly also calling a hit on her very own mother. Shange met the family in Bushbuckrigde this past week. NALEDI: It's a family that's literally been torn apart by all of these murders and attempted murders. One of the questions that I asked was how she feels towards her sister. And she answered. I never thought that one day she would want to prey on me. VO: In an interesting twist, Ndlovu’s mother testified in her defence - despite allegedly being one of her daughter’s targets. GIADA: no one wants to believe that their child is capable of doing something like this // even to conceptualise the fact that one of your children would be responsible for the murder of your other children and your grand children - I think that’s very hard for someone // there’ a large amount of denial// VO: While the state has wrapped up its case, Ndlovu has maintained her innocence, pleading not guilty on all charges. NALEDI: Around 51 state witnesses have testified, and according to Nomia, all 51 of them have lied at one point or the other. //Everyone has lied. That is her story. VO: The prosecution presented what seems to be a comprehensive case with a range of witnesses connecting the dots in Ndlovu’s alleged web of deception . De Klerk adds the insurance industry’s forensic teams determined the quantum of claims. GARTH: The South African police services// gathered evidence on her and then they approached us to say, Please, can we tie together //from the insurance point of view //how many insurance claims had she put together. there's a whole tree around it as to where the money went how it flowed and who were the ultimate beneficiaries. VO: WIth public interest growing in the case, it appeared that Ndlovu was playing into the spotlight. NALEDI: She's completely flipped scripts. VO: Her timing was impeccable if not suspicious, notes Shange. NALEDI: We’ve noticed is that her falling ill and her being unable to stand the heat in the courtroom is sometimes usually comes at a very crucial time during the state's questioning VO: Del Fabbro observed that Ndlovu’s antics could be a manipulative attempt to tip the scales in her favour. GIADA: It may be that she could be trying to be perceived as perhaps unstable. // although it’ll be very difficult to argue for given the meticulous and calculated ways that those crimes were planned out. VO: The alleged crimes have left the families of the victims gripped by fear. NALEDI: The thing about Nomia’s Network, we have no idea how far it stretches. JUSTICE: What if she doesn't get the full conviction? We as the family, we are not safe VO: Del Fabbro observes serial killers who kill for money, often view people as a means to an end. GIADA: We are talking about personality structure which is not very capable of empathy //and who really is about surviving and meeting her own needs at any cost. And in this case, the cost was her family. CLAIRE REMORSE? GIADA: Wouldn't hold my breath. // you may see self-pity, but you won't see remorse. It will look the same, potentially. Although I think if you spent enough time, you'd see that it's quite superficial. VO: Ndlovu’s showmanship is not winning over any fans. JUSTICE: The way in which is just she's taking everyone or the courts for for a ride, It's it's so it's so painful I never suspected that she would be this. This this mean, this, evil. VO: Even with Ndlovu on trial, Nhlapo doubts whether a conviction will ever bring him peace. JABU: I don't think that's enough because I'm I'm being taxed money to pay her food at prison that hurts me. metadata.Summary: While the country is gripped by the antics unfolding in a Gauteng Court around the case of former police constable Nomia Rosemary Ndlovu, an alleged serial killer accused of murdering her family members in return for insurance payouts, we dig deeper into the driving forces behind women who kill.
